column2: What are the primary learning-related use-cases for AI tools described by dyslexic learners in online discussions?
column3: How do dyslexic users describe the role of assistive technology accommodations like laptops for exams, extra time, or browser extensions in supporting their learning?
column4: What specific reading-support features, such as coloured overlays, reading guides, bionic reading, or adjustable spacing, do dyslexic users describe as more helpful than font changes alone?
column5: How is AI described as part of everyday study routines compared with one-off or occasional use?
column6: How do reported AI use-cases differ between school, university, and work-related learning contexts?
column7: In what ways do learners use AI to support idea generation, task understanding, or organisation of thoughts during study?

column2: What benefits and failure modes do dyslexic learners report when using AI tools for different learning tasks?
column3: When do users describe AI outputs as inaccurate, too generic, confusing, or not aligned with what they were trying to express?
column4: In what ways do learners describe AI as helping them participate more effectively in education or work-based learning environments?
column5: In what situations do users describe AI as offering limited value compared with other assistive tools, accommodations, or personal coping strategies?
column6: What concerns do dyslexic learners raise about over-reliance on AI, reduced skill development, or uncertainty about whether they are really learning?
column7: How do learners describe AI improving clarity, confidence, or speed when completing learning-related work?

column2: Under what conditions are AI tools described as helpful, supportive, or inclusive for dyslexic learners?
column3: How do parents of dyslexic or dysgraphic children describe their experiences building, seeking, or customizing AI tools when existing solutions and school accommodations fall short?
column4: What role do accessibility, ease of use, and low effort play in whether AI tools are experienced as inclusive?
column5: How do dyslexic learners and their families describe negotiating with schools or teachers to gain acceptance of AI tools, dictation, or typing as legitimate accommodations rather than as shortcuts?
column6: What user practices, such as prompting, checking outputs, or combining AI with other tools, are associated with more positive experiences?
column7: How do task type, context, or severity of difficulty shape whether AI is perceived as supportive?

column2: How are AI-based supports discussed in relation to broader educational challenges and support structures, including institutional accommodations and personal coping strategies?
column3: In what ways is AI discussed as complementing, replacing, or compensating for existing support structures?
column4: What gaps in school, university, or workplace support lead learners to turn to AI tools?
column5: How do dyslexic learners describe the legitimacy and acceptance of AI-based accommodations within formal IEPs or institutional support plans compared to traditional accommodations like extra time or dictation?
column6: How are concerns about fairness, legitimacy, or dependency discussed when AI is used alongside institutional accommodations?
column7: How do learners position AI within their wider personal coping strategies for reading, writing, organisation, or communication?

column2: How have discussions of AI tools among dyslexic learners changed over time in terms of prevalence, tone, and perceived role in learning support?
column3: What do dyslexic learners say about community attitudes, rules, or skepticism toward AI-built tools, and how does this affect their willingness to try or recommend such tools?
column4: How have perceived benefits and risks of AI evolved as these tools have become more widely available?
column5: How has the volume of AI-related discussion among dyslexic learners changed over time?
column6: How have the main reported uses of AI shifted over time, for example from general curiosity to everyday academic or workplace support?
column7: How has the role of AI in dyslexia-related support changed over time relative to broader discussions of technology, accommodations, and coping strategies?
